cards.front: What is the geometric interpretation of the determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix with columns $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$?
cards.back: It represents the signed area of the parallelogram formed by the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.

cards.front: In the context of "signed volume," what does the "sign" (positive or negative) indicate?
cards.back: The sign indicates the orientation of the basis formed by the vectors. For 3D, a positive sign typically means a right-handed orientation, and a negative sign means a left-handed orientation, relative to the standard basis.

cards.front: Given three vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, how is the signed volume of the parallelepiped they define calculated?
cards.back:
Form a matrix $A$ where the columns (or rows) are $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3$. The signed volume is then $\det(A)$.
$$ A = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & | \\ \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 & \mathbf{v}_3 \\ | & | & | \end{pmatrix} \implies \text{Signed Volume} = \det(A) $$

cards.front: If the determinant of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ is $\det(A) < 0$, what does this tell us about the orientation of the column vectors of $A$?
cards.back: The column vectors of $A$ form a left-handed system (or basis), meaning their orientation is opposite to that of the standard basis vectors (which form a right-handed system).

cards.front: Geometrically, what does a signed volume of zero for a set of vectors imply about their linear dependence?
cards.back: A signed volume of zero implies that the vectors are linearly dependent. This means they do not span the full $n$-dimensional space (e.g., 3 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are coplanar or collinear, forming a "flat" or "collapsed" shape).

cards.front: Explain how the determinant of a transformation matrix $T$ relates to the scaling of volume in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
cards.back: The absolute value of the determinant, $|\det(T)|$, represents the factor by which $T$ scales any $n$-dimensional volume. The signed determinant $\det(T)$ also indicates whether the transformation preserves or reverses the orientation of space. For example, the unit hypercube is transformed into a parallelepiped whose signed volume is $\det(T)$.

cards.front: How does swapping two adjacent column vectors in a matrix affect the signed volume of the parallelepiped they define?
cards.back: Swapping two adjacent column vectors (or any two columns) of a matrix changes the orientation of the basis, which results in negating the determinant. Thus, the signed volume also changes its sign. For example, $\det(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3) = - \det(\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_3)$.
